concepts.decision: Separate pipeline roles/environments and define required evidence and authorization before promotion.
concepts.definition: Automated and governed continuous integration/continuous delivery pipeline practices that build, test, package, and promote change through environments.
concepts.failureExample: A pipeline credential able to alter source, build, and production creates an unchecked path to deployment.
concepts.label: Ci Cd

concepts.decision: Use to discover integration defects quickly while protecting the source revision and test environment.
concepts.definition: Frequent integration of changes into a shared codebase with automated build and test feedback.
concepts.failureExample: Passing a unit build does not prove the merged application or release artifact is authorized.
concepts.label: Continuous Integration

concepts.decision: Require explicit policy/approval and environment safeguards even when deployment can be automated.
concepts.definition: Capability to keep validated changes ready for controlled production release, with promotion evidence and release decisions.
concepts.failureExample: Automatically releasing every ready artifact can expose customers to an unreviewed high-impact change.
concepts.label: Continuous Delivery

concepts.decision: Name artifacts and allowable states, control entry/change, and preserve the baseline needed for rollback and investigation.
concepts.definition: Control of identified configuration items, versions, authorized changes, baselines, status, and reproducibility.
concepts.failureExample: An unknown production configuration makes it impossible to reproduce, verify, or safely reverse a release.
concepts.label: Configuration Management

concepts.decision: Use isolated/maintained runners, constrained identities, protected configuration, logs, and response procedures for suspected compromise.
concepts.definition: Assurance that the build process, runner, inputs, configuration, and outputs were protected from unauthorized alteration.
concepts.failureExample: A compromised build runner can inject code after source review and before artifact signing.
concepts.label: Build Integrity

concepts.decision: Verify digest/attestation/signing and promotion records before deployment; preserve enough evidence to investigate or reproduce.
concepts.definition: Evidence linking a released artifact to its source revision, dependencies, build process, identity, tests, and authorized promotion.
concepts.failureExample: An artifact name and version label alone cannot prove what source or builder produced it.
concepts.label: Artifact Provenance

concepts.decision: Use early to find code-pattern issues and triage findings with context; it cannot prove runtime configuration or all exploitability.
concepts.definition: Static application security testing analyzes source, bytecode, or representations without executing the application.
concepts.failureExample: Treating SAST silence as proof of secure authentication misses deployment and business-logic failures.
concepts.label: Sast

concepts.decision: Use against a controlled, representative running target and interpret coverage/authorization limits.
concepts.definition: Dynamic application security testing exercises a running application from outside to observe security behavior.
concepts.failureExample: A DAST scan that lacks an authenticated role cannot establish that privileged authorization is sound.
concepts.label: Dast

concepts.decision: Use with dependency inventory, provenance, version policy, and remediation ownership; distinguish known-CVE status from integrity and fitness.
concepts.definition: Software composition analysis identifies included third-party components and associated known-risk/license information.
concepts.failureExample: A clean SCA result does not prove the dependency came from an approved source or has no unknown flaw.
concepts.label: Sca

concepts.decision: Use when instrumented execution can enrich code/runtime insight; define test coverage and protect the instrumented environment.
concepts.definition: Interactive application security testing observes application behavior from inside while tests execute.
concepts.failureExample: IAST cannot observe an abuse path that its test suite never executes.
concepts.label: Iast

concepts.decision: Map and protect each trust dependency and define response for compromised source, dependency, builder, key, or repository.
concepts.definition: The people, code, dependencies, tools, build systems, repositories, services, and handoffs that contribute to delivered software.
concepts.failureExample: Focusing only on application code ignores a malicious package, stolen release key, or altered pipeline configuration.
concepts.label: Software Supply Chain

concepts.decision: Preserve source/dependency/build/identity/attestation evidence sufficient to verify origin and investigate anomalies.
concepts.definition: Verifiable history of where software inputs/artifacts came from and how they were transformed before release.
concepts.failureExample: Without provenance, an organization cannot distinguish an approved artifact from one substituted in the repository.
concepts.label: Software Provenance

concepts.decision: Pin/record versions where appropriate, review source/license/vulnerability status, assign owners, and test updates before promotion.
concepts.definition: Selection, inventory, version control, review, update, and retirement of software components a product relies on.
concepts.failureExample: An unconstrained transitive update can change production behavior without a deliberate code change.
concepts.label: Dependency Management

misconceptions.claim: A clean SAST report proves the release is secure.
misconceptions.correction: It cannot cover runtime configuration, dependency provenance, deployment identity, or all dynamic and business-logic abuse.

misconceptions.claim: A signed artifact or SBOM proves the release has no supply-chain risk.
misconceptions.correction: Signatures and inventories need verified identity, protected keys, approved source/dependency policy, traceable build and deployment evidence, revocation, and incident response.

outcome: Design layered pipeline controls that produce trustworthy, traceable release artifacts.

sections.body: CI/CD pipelines should isolate source, build, test, staging, and production privileges; protect runners and configuration; pin and inventory dependencies; preserve logs and provenance; and require authorized promotion. Configuration management detects drift and makes rollback reproducible.
keyPoints: A compromised runner can alter every downstream artifact.
Promotion boundaries reduce unauthorized release risk.
Provenance links artifact identity to source, dependencies, builder, tests, and approver.
sections.title: Separate and attest pipeline stages

sections.body: SAST inspects code or representations before execution; DAST exercises a running application; SCA inventories third-party components; IAST observes execution while tests run. Select tests from risk and lifecycle timing, interpret findings, assign remediation, and retain evidence rather than treating any tool as complete coverage.
keyPoints: Static, dynamic, composition, and interactive tests expose different blind spots.
Tools generate signals; triage and risk ownership determine release action.
Tests must cover APIs, configurations, dependencies, and abuse cases where relevant.
sections.title: Use complementary application-security tests

sections.body: A secure build and release process identifies the approved source revision, dependencies and their provenance, build environment, build steps, test and policy results, produced artifact, signing identity, repository, deployment approval, and the evidence that connects them. Protect source and pipeline credentials, separate or constrain roles, pin and verify dependencies where appropriate, preserve logs and attestations, and define how keys, compromised builders, malicious dependencies, or a failed rollback are handled. An SBOM can describe components, but it does not alone prove a component is safe, the artifact came from the intended source, or deployment followed policy. NIST SSDF’s Protect the Software and Produce Well-Secured Software practices provide a risk-informed structure; OWASP Top 10:2025 addresses software supply chain failures and software or data integrity failures as awareness risks; the list is not a complete verification standard.
keyPoints: Integrity evidence should allow a reviewer to trace a deployed artifact back to approved source, dependencies, build, test, signing, and release decision.
An inventory or signature is useful only with trustworthy identity, scope, verification, revocation, and response processes.
sections.title: Make release integrity a verifiable chain, not a vendor promise

options.feedback: Changed fact: A dependency is republished under a valid-looking signature from a compromised but previously trusted publisher identity, and affected versions may already be deployed. Why this answer fails: “Reuse the original conclusion because the overall control family is unchanged” does not account for that changed condition. Corrected consequence: Restrict artifact writes, sign or attest provenance, verify identity at promotion, bind deployment to approved commit and test evidence, triage high-risk findings, and provide rollback. Repair target: Decision recomputed — Affected promotion is frozen while build and deployment records identify prior artifacts; trusted publisher and integrity policy are revalidated before a clean rebuild.
